one_liner: AVX2 vector-quantization library that encodes float vectors into 4-bit codes and computes approximate distances and dot products far faster than PQ or exact float math.
what_it_does: Bolt (Blalock and Guttag, KDD 2017) learns a quantizer from training data, compresses each float vector into 8, 16 or 32 bytes of 4-bit codes, and then answers squared-L2 distance, dot-product, k-NN and maximum-inner-product queries directly on the compressed codes. The C++ API is a BoltEncoder class (set_centroids, set_data, dists_sq, dot_prods, knn_l2, knn_mips) plus templated free functions bolt_encode, bolt_lut and bolt_scan; a SWIG Python wrapper exposes bolt.Encoder(reduction='dot'|'l2').fit(X).transform(q). It is not a drop-in GEMM or BLAS replacement: results are approximate, shifted and scaled uint16 values, not floats.
how_it_is_fast: Product-quantization style encoding with K = 16 centroids per subspace instead of PQ's 256, so each code is 4 bits and a 16-entry lookup table fits in one 128-bit lane; the scan does table lookups with vpshufb (_mm256_shuffle_epi8) on 32 codes at a time, accumulating with saturating 8-bit or 16-bit adds and writing with non-temporal stores. Query lookup tables are quantized from float to uint8 with a learned per-table offset and scale (quantile-based, so outliers do not blow the range), and codes are stored in 32-row column-major blocks so one 256-bit load feeds 32 rows. Much of the encoding and table-build speedup over PQ is the K = 16 choice itself: for D = 128 and 16 bytes, Bolt evaluates 32 codebooks x 16 centroids x 4 dimensions (2,048 multiply-adds) against PQ's 16 x 256 x 8 (32,768), a 16x reduction in work before any SIMD (derived from the profile constants).
when_to_use: Large collections of mostly dense float vectors (embeddings, descriptors) where approximate L2 distances or dot products are acceptable and memory or scan throughput is the bottleneck: the repo's D = 128, 16-byte run scans about 1.26 billion uint8 distances per second (1e6 codes in 0.79 ms) on one core.

Batch encoding of many vectors: 10,000 128-dimensional vectors encode to 16-byte codes in 2.29 ms (about 4.4 million vectors/s, about 2.2 GB/s of float input, derived) against 39.8 ms for the repo's own PQ encoder.

Candidate generation for nearest-neighbour or maximum-inner-product search, followed by exact re-ranking of the top hits, since the slides say Bolt has to retrieve more points than PQ/OPQ for a given compression level.

Approximate matrix products where one operand is reused many times and the error is tolerable: the square matmul timings run 5.8x faster than single-threaded Eigen at N = 512 and 57x at N = 8192 without re-encoding (3.4x and 38x when the matrix is encoded inside the timed call).
x86-64 servers or desktops with AVX2 (Haswell, 2013, or later) where you can build C++14 sources directly.
when_not_to_use: You need exact results or float outputs: Bolt returns quantized uint16 scores, its dot products are 'slightly less accurate than others' per the authors' slides, and 8-bit scans saturate at 255.
Small problems: below N = 128 the square matmul is slower than Eigen (N = 64: 0.024 ms with encoding vs 0.009 ms), and the speedup needs enough rows to amortize table construction.

ARM, Apple Silicon or any non-AVX2 target: the kernels are AVX2-only; the README invites ARM contributions (issue #2), issue #23 asking for other vector instruction sets is still open, and issue #25 reports an install failure on an M1 Mac.
Python-first projects that need a working package: the README says the Python wrapper 'seems to be no longer building' for many people (issues #4, #15, #31, #37), and it is slower than the C++ path.
You need a maintained library: the last commit is from June 2022, open issues from 2022 to 2025 (#35, #37, #39, #40, #41) have no fix, and FAISS was never benchmarked against it in the repo.

integration.dependencies: Eigen (vendored in cpp/src/external); SWIG and NumPy for the Python wrapper; Bazel for the provided build (or the Xcode project the author used)
integration.min_toolchain: C++14 (Bazel copts: -O3 -march=native -mavx -ffast-math -std=c++14); only tested with Clang on OS X per experiments/README
integration.thread_safety: not documented; all kernels are single-threaded free functions and BoltEncoder holds mutable state (codes, lookup tables), so share one encoder across threads only with external locking

gotchas: Layout and size constraints: bolt_encode requires nrows to be a multiple of 32, ncols divisible by 2 x NBytes and a 32-byte-aligned output buffer, and bolt_scan writes with _mm256_stream_si256, so its output must be 32-byte aligned too; issue #35 (open) reports a general protection fault from an aligned _mm256_load_ps in the repo's AVX sgemm helper when given a non-aligned stride.

The square-matmul speedups grow with N partly because code length is fixed: Bolt's cost is about N^2 x (16 + M) against GEMM's N^3, so at N = 8192 Bolt<8> represents each 8,192-float row with 16 four-bit codes (512 dimensions per codebook). The profile runs on random codes, centroids and offsets and measures speed only, so accuracy at those sizes is never shown.

Harness weaknesses in cpp/test/quantize/profile_bolt.cpp: _run_bolt_matmul takes the centroid, code, lookup-table and output matrices by value (the ColMatrix codes are even converted to RowMatrix on each call, and the 134 MB uint16 output is copied at N = 8192), so the product is written into a temporary copy while the anti-dead-code check prevent_optimizing_away_dists reads the caller's untouched out matrix; nothing proves the scan ran, although times rising with code length (231, 252 and 306 ms for 8, 16 and 32 bytes at N = 8192) suggest it did. The 'bolt scan uint16 safe' row is written bolt_scan<(M, true)>(...), a comma expression that sets NBytes to 1, so in the current source that row times a 1-byte scan (it is not one of the catalogued numbers).

Correctness bug in an unbenchmarked path: in the uint16 bolt_scan with SignedLUTs = true, the even-indexed lanes are computed as _mm256_srai_epi16(_mm256_srai_epi16(x, 8), 8), which yields the sign of the odd byte instead of the sign-extended low byte (_mm256_srai_epi16(_mm256_slli_epi16(x, 8), 8)), so half of the rows get wrong scores with signed lookup tables; the matmul and scan timings use unsigned tables and are unaffected.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Bolt over PQ Fast Scan or Quick ADC (technicolor-research) when encoding speed and approximate dot products or matrix products matter as much as scan speed, since Bolt also vectorizes encoding and quantizes its lookup tables with learned offsets; pick PQ Fast Scan when you must return exactly the same results as a standard PQ scan, which Bolt's 4-bit codes and 8-bit tables do not.
verified_claims_summary: First-party Catch timing dumps (best of 5, 10 repetitions; the paper snippet names one thread on a 2013 MacBook Pro with a 2.6 GHz Core i7-4960HQ and Clang/Xcode builds) show Bolt with 8-byte codes computing an approximate uint16 N x N product 1.4x (N = 128) to 57x (N = 8192) faster than an exact float32 Eigen GEMM, and encoding 10,000 128-dimensional vectors in 2.29 ms against 39.8 ms for the repo's own PQ; Eigen's 13.19 s at N = 8192 is about 83 GFLOP/s, consistent with one AVX2/FMA core (derived from page data).
status_note: Abandoned research code since June 2022 (the MADDNESS successor 'mithral' lives in the same repo) but MPL-2.0 and small enough to vendor as C++14 source for AVX2 machines; the Python package is not reliably buildable.
sources_read: WebSearch snippet of arXiv 1706.10283 (experimental setup: single thread, 2013 MacBook Pro, Core i7-4960HQ, best of 5 averaged over 10 trials)
